Pakistan's Mohammad Rizwan and Babar Azam in action at the 2023 Cricket World Cup [Adnan Abidi/Reuters]By AFPPublished On 21 Nov 202621 Nov 2026
Pakistan’s Cricket Board has announced that it will drop former captains Mohammad Rizwan and Shan Masood in a major overhaul of its central contract list.
Saturday’s announcement, which expands the pool of contracted players to 38 ⁠from 30, comes a day after Pakistan won the second Test against Sri Lanka in Rawalpindi, marking a first series win in two years.

“We are testing new players and these contracts are devised to let players focus on their specific format,” Pakistan selector Aaqib Javed told the media.
The board overhauled the Test squad after the second Test in its disastrous 3-0 defeat against England, sending seven players home and sacking head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed.
White-ball head coach Mike Hesson was given the Test team in a bid to lift the country, which is currently ninth and last in the 2025-27 World Test Championship cycle.
Besides Rizwan and Masood, white-ball specialist Saim Ayub, spinner Noman Ali and pace bowler Hasan Ali are among the 12 players who have been removed from contracts.
Test skipper Babar Azam and recently sacked Twenty20 International (T20I) skipper Salman Agha are in the top category of the 38-player list.

Military units of the Coalition of the Willing forces take part in Koalicja 26.2, the coalition's first full-scale multinational military exercise, in Nowa Deba, Poland [Omar Marques/Getty Images]By Heba HabibPublished On 21 Nov 202621 Nov 2026
Security cameras captured the moment a suspected Russian missile struck Polish territory during an attack on Ukraine on Friday. Poland’s government says it may have been hit by two missiles and a jet-powered drone.
The incident, which took place as European troops held military drills in the country and as the United States pushes to revive talks on ending the war in Ukraine, have raised questions about whether the strike was deliberate.

So what happened, and does this mean Russia has struck Poland, a NATO member?
What happened in Poland?
Poland’s Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference in Warsaw that two missiles and a jet-powered drone fell on Polish territory during Russia’s overnight attack on November 20. The missiles came down at Nowy Lipowiec and Rudnik nad Sanem, while the jet-powered drone fell at Molodycz, all in the country’s southeast.
One missile is believed to have crashed about 35km (22 miles) from where European troops’ military exercises were taking place. A Kh-101 cruise missile went down about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border, and what officials believe was a jet-powered drone hit about 30km (20 miles) from the border. No immediate injuries or damage were reported.

Usman Khawaja and David Warner were taken off television commentary duties on Saturday until the “Sandpapergate” storm passes, with both set to miss Australia’s entire Twenty20 series against England.
The retired pair have been the centre of attention since Khawaja claimed in his autobiography more than two weeks ago that the whole team knew about the plot to alter the ball in a Test against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018.

Only then-captain Steve Smith, his deputy Warner and Cameron Bancroft – who used the sandpaper – were found to be responsible by a Cricket Australia probe.
The move by Fox Sports, for whom they both work, came after Cricket Australia threw its “unanimous support” behind embattled Test captain Pat Cummins.
Cummins denied he knew what was going on and has been under huge pressure since Khawaja’s claims, which were first backed by Warner and then Bancroft.

Israel has issued orders to demolish two buildings in Hebron in Area A of the occupied West Bank [Sari Jaradat/Al Jazeera]By Fayha ShalashPublished On 21 Nov 202621 Nov 2026
Hebron, Occupied West Bank – Amjad al-Qawasmi stood gazing at the eight-storey residential building he constructed 13 years ago in the heart of Hebron. He struggled to understand how it could be reduced to rubble in a matter of moments.
The building in the southern West Bank is one of two upon which the Israeli army posted demolition notices last Sunday morning, even though both are in Area A, which, under the Oslo Accords, is under full Palestinian control.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Israel takes measures to crush Palestinian business in occupied West Banklist 2 of 3As homes seized, Jericho’s Palestinian residents fear settler takeoverlist 3 of 3Israeli court upholds detention of Palestinian land activist Ghassan Najjarend of list
The buildings are in the Dairat al-Seer area, in the northwest of Hebron. One contains 25 residential apartments, the other has 40, alongside an adjacent home. The Israeli army has set a one-week deadline for filing objections to the demolition orders.
The Israeli authorities justified the decisions by citing the buildings’ proximity to “Settler Road 35”, despite the structures possessing all the necessary permits from the Palestinian Authority and the Hebron Municipality.
Hebron is divided into a larger area under Palestinian administrative control and a smaller area – housing Israeli settlers – in the centre of the city.

Activists from Stop Killer Robots, a coalition of nongovernmental organisations opposing lethal autonomous weapons, stage a protest [File: Annegret Hilse/Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff and AFPPublished On 21 Nov 202621 Nov 2026
The 128 countries at a United Nations conference in the Swiss city of Geneva have agreed to “elaborate” on a possible accord regulating lethal autonomous weapons, known as “killer robots”, in the next two years.
Saturday’s announcement at the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) came after nearly 100 nations pushed for swift adoption of legally binding rules on the weapons capable of killing without a human making the final decision to fire.

Key arms-producing nations, including the United States, Russia and Israel, opposed the push. Decisions under the convention require the agreement of all member states.
Diplomats said Russia’s objections over procedure led to some formal sessions being called off. Talks over the final wording then ran through the night.
Julien Thoeni, the Swiss diplomat who chaired the conference, said some countries had rejected the word “negotiate”. The agreed text refers instead to the “elaboration” of an instrument.
He said more than 10 years of talks had produced a significant step for humanitarian disarmament.
“It shows that even in today’s deeply divided world, multilateral diplomacy can still deliver concrete results,” he told reporters as the meeting wrapped up.
